newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal mulls how to spend privatisation windfall.
newsitem.headline: Portugal mulls how to spend privatisation windfall.

text.p: Portugal's Socialist government will enjoy a larger than expected windfall from privatisations this year to spend on public investment or reducing state debt, analysts said on Tuesday.

Prime Minister Antonio Guterres said in New York earlier this month that the state could raise 450 billion escudos ($2.91 billion) from privatisations in 1996, well above its target of 380 billion ($2.46 billion).
Three more privatisations are outstanding this year.
On Monday Portuguese, Spanish and French companies submitted sealed bids in the privatisation of Portugal's biggest tobacco producer Tabaqueira, a senior finance ministry official said.
The government plans to sell a 65 percent stake by public competition at a minimum price of 4,650 escudos ($30) a share. The bids were due to be opened in a public ceremony on Tuesday.
The pre-registration period is under way for the sale of a 45 percent stake in Cimpor-Cimentos de Portugal SA, Portugal's biggest cement producer, on October 15.
The government must also sell its 13.2 percent stake in Banco Totta e Acoresby the end of the year.

The main contributions to privatisation earnings so far this year came from Portugal Telecom, which raked in almost $1 billion, and Banco de Fomento e Exterior, sold to Banco Portugues de Investimentofor $900 million.
"The government must decide how to spend this money -- by reducing public debt or increasing investment," said Isabel Cabral, economist with Lisbon broker Fincor.

Mark Howard of Lloyds Bank Fund Managers in Cascais told Reuters that next year's regional elections in Portugal should encourage the Socialist authorities to spend some of the windfall on upgrading public infrastructure.
"It also depends on Portugal's progress in meeting targets for joining the European single currency," he said.

The government has expressed optimism that it could cut the budget deficit, one of the criteria for entry to the European Union's single currency, to four percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year, below its targeted 4.2 percent.
It has said the level of public debt should drop to 70.5 percent of GDP this year from 71.6 percent in 1995.
Analysts said the privatisations slated for the remainder of the year should succeed.
Tabaqueira should attract a good price as three bidders were vying to control Portugal's dominant cigarette manufacturer.
"Tabaqueira is attractive because it has a near-monopoly in its market," said Howard.

The bids were submitted by Spanish firm Tabacalera, in partnership with Portugal's Empresa Madeirense de Tabacos, as well as French company Seita and Portugal's Jorge de Mello industrial group, said Jose Martins de Sa, president of the jury presiding over the privatisation.

The privatisation of Cimpor, which could be worth more than 120 billion escudos ($776 million), will be comfortably oversubscribed as it enjoys a healthy construction sector in the run-up to Lisbon's Expo 98 World Fair, analysts said.
Cimpor officials have said the company could use its cash mountain to buy foreign cement producers after the selloff.

The government should have no difficulty placing its stake in Totta as it is part of businessman Antonio Champalimaud's extensive banking and insurance group that has good potential for growth, analysts said. $1=154.45 escudos
